title: The silence of God
hook: Psalm 22 and the cross both hold God's silence

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: John of the Cross and a mother weaning her child from the sweetness. Your line was night is working. Where did you stay with something dry for one more minute? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

"O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent." That's the second verse of Psalm twenty-two, a song addressed to the chief musician, set down by someone who has called out day and night and heard nothing back. Some people live that line long before they find it in the Bible: the phone that doesn't ring, the prayer that seems to hit the ceiling. And this is the psalm Jesus reaches for on the cross. Today: the silence of God.

First, the psalm names silence honestly. It doesn't pretend God answered. It says, plainly, thou hearest not. And that line was kept in the Psalms, where it could be prayed instead of hidden. Second, the cross. Matthew records Jesus crying out, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the opening words of this same psalm. At his baptism, Matthew says, a voice spoke from heaven. Here, at the cross, the Gospel records no voice in reply. Only the cry, and then, soon after, his death. Christians have read this moment in different ways: some hear Jesus truly feeling abandoned; others note he's praying a psalm that turns to trust. Some hold both. Third, where the psalm goes. Keep reading Psalm twenty-two and it turns. Further on it says God "hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard." The same psalm that began with thou hearest not comes round to he heard. For the psalmist, silence wasn't the same as absence. Last, a day of silence on the calendar. Between Good Friday and Easter morning comes Holy Saturday. In some churches the altar is stripped bare and the bells stay quiet. Nothing is announced. The body lies in the tomb. Lamentations has a line for days like that: "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD." The churches that mark it keep that waiting on purpose. Silence is not absence.

Here's the practice: sit in silence and wait. Settle, and breathe. Let the room go quiet. Don't fill it: no music, no words, no list. If a question has been sitting in you without an answer, let it be there, unanswered, in the quiet. Notice that silence has a texture: a hum, a breath, a car far away. If you pray, you can wait before God without saying anything at all. If you don't, wait anyway, and let the quiet be enough. The bell holds the time.
The silence of God. The stretch when prayer seems to meet nothing, prayed in Psalm twenty-two and on the cross, and kept each year on Holy Saturday.
Your line: silence is not absence. Today, give someone the gift of your silence: let them finish, let a pause stay a pause, and don't rush to fill it. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 22 in Holy Week, and on Holy Saturday some churches strip the altar, silence the bells and hold no ordinary service until the Easter Vigil, keeping the day as one of waiting.

fork.setup: you're standing near the cross, and you hear Jesus cry out: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani. what are those words?
options: a new prayer no one had heard before.
the opening of Psalm 22: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
words with no meaning at all.
fork.reveal: Matthew gives the cry as the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that says thou hearest not and later turns to he heard. Jesus prays the silence in the psalm's own words.

original.note: Hebrew: my God, the first word of Psalm 22, which Matthew gives on Jesus's lips as Eli.

trapdoor: what you thought: if God is silent, God isn't there.
what it means: Psalm 22 and the cross both pray into silence, and the psalm goes on to say God heard.
what a scholar hears: Matthew gives the cry as Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani, the opening of Psalm 22. some readers hear the whole psalm, turning to trust, behind the first line.

notes: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani (Hebrew and Aramaic mixed) is quoted as Matthew gives it, without a language claim.
'Written to be sung' for Psalm 22 rests on its heading (to the chief Musician); confirm.
Holy Saturday customs (stripped altar, silent bells, no ordinary service until the Easter Vigil) vary by church; attributed to 'some churches'. Confirm.
Psalm 22:24 is quoted from 'hath not despised'; the verse begins 'For he hath not despised'. Confirm.
Day 1380 (A God who suffers) may also use the cry from the cross; this day focuses on silence and the psalm's ending to avoid repeating it.

Editor pass: verse 24 is not the psalm's last line, so 'by the end' / 'ends with he heard' became 'further on' / 'comes round to' / 'turns' in spoken, screen, match and trapdoor; 'written to be sung' now rests on the heading ('to the chief musician'); cut 'not a doubter's complaint from outside the faith', which echoed day 1377's 'that isn't a skeptic'; replaced the fork (day 1379 already asked the listener to write the last line of a dark song) and the 'ends the way it begins' myth (close to day 1379's Psalm 88 myth); softened 'Christians pray Psalm 22 especially in Holy Week' and 'Christians keep that waiting day' to some churches.
Audit: the purpose claim about why the Bible kept the line, and "silence wasn't the same as absence" as a flat statement, now attributed to the psalm and the psalmist.
